claims.statement: dcode discovers user and project MCP configurations in ascending precedence, merges by server name, and treats an explicit configuration as the highest-precedence source whose load errors are fatal.

dcode applies project MCP trust after precedence resolves the winning definition: user-owned scoped approvals or whole-project trust can enable it, explicit deny wins, and an unreadable trust policy disables whole-project trust.
dcode's `MCPSessionManager` retains FastMCP router and backend resources across loads so in-flight tools survive a reload, then performs bounded best-effort cleanup of all retained loads.

dcode isolates validation, preflight, connection, and tool-construction failures per MCP server, redacting details for configurations that interpolate environment values and reporting outcomes as `MCPServerInfo` metadata.

dcode persists disabled MCP server names in `[mcp].disabled_servers`; names apply across same-named configurations, disabled servers are skipped before connection, and unreadable managed deny policy fails closed by disabling every server.

`resolve_mcp_server_env` returns a deep-copied per-server configuration and expands only braced `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` references in command, URL, arguments, environment, headers, and OAuth settings; malformed references and unset required values fail activation.

For remote MCP servers, dcode uses explicit OAuth configuration or stored OAuth tokens unless a static `Authorization` header overrides them; explicit OAuth with no stored token is reported as an unauthenticated server without attempting connection.

dcode exports MCP tools with deterministic provider-safe names while retaining original identities in metadata, then applies exactly one `allowedTools` or `disabledTools` filter using literal or glob matches against original and exported names; unmatched filter entries warn without blocking startup.

A truly stateless dcode MCP load releases its discovery manager and reconnects the owning server for each tool invocation, whereas an externally supplied `MCPSessionManager` adopts the connected load and takes precedence over stateless conversion.

dcode treats a project `.env` as untrusted: it blocks both generic execution-affecting variables and project-level MCP trust/approval controls before they reach the active environment, preventing a repository from self-approving its own MCP definition.

Project dotenv loading is controlled by `startup.read_project_dotenv` with managed, process-environment, trusted-global-dotenv, TOML, and default precedence; the toggle is read before the project file, and an unreadable global dotenv fails closed by skipping the project file.

`FileTokenStorage` isolates MCP OAuth credentials by safe server identity and resolved endpoint/client identity, persists tokens with an absolute expiry sidecar, serializes same-file mutations, atomically replaces files, and attempts user-only token-file permissions.

The expiry-aware MCP OAuth provider restores stored expiry and OAuth metadata on initialization, schedules refresh before expiry, and serializes refresh grants with a cross-process per-token-file lock that reloads storage before refreshing to prevent rotating refresh-token reuse.

The `dcode mcp` command group provides `login` and `config`: bare login lists OAuth servers with no stored token and signals indeterminate state through its exit code, targeted login uses the trust-gated resolved configuration or an explicitly selected config, and config only reports discovery paths without opening files.

Interactive OAuth login accepts only remote HTTP/SSE MCP transports, resolves environment values before deriving token storage identity, forces a new authorization flow without deleting a working stored token, and falls back from unavailable browser/loopback callback handling to an authorization URL and pasted callback.

The local TUI's `/mcp` viewer exposes login-capable OAuth servers, persistent disable toggles, and reconnect requests; after a successful login it marks tools as awaiting reconnect and restarts the app-owned LangGraph server immediately or after an active task, while refusing login against a remote server it cannot restart.

The LangGraph server preloads MCP metadata separately for the local TUI, then uses stateless discovery with a process-wide session manager bound to the server event loop so real backend sessions are created lazily for tool invocation.

Routine MCP loading builds OAuth providers in non-interactive mode, whose reauthorization handlers do not prompt; servers without usable credentials are instead reported as unauthenticated, including OAuth challenges and failed refresh credentials.

Focused MCP command tests cover trust-gated resolution, login-list exit behavior, resolved URL token identity, and corrupt token reporting, while OAuth tests cover token storage isolation, permissions, concurrent persistence, expiry state, and refresh behavior.

Talon loads one selected MCP configuration, validates and resolves enabled definitions before connection, supports stdio, SSE, and streamable HTTP transports, and contains each enabled server's load failure as an `error` or `unauthenticated` status so sibling servers can load.

Talon rejects dangerous stdio environment variables and prevents combining OAuth with a static Authorization header, limiting configuration paths that could alter subprocess execution or send OAuth credentials ambiguously.

Talon's `MCPToolProvider` adds server-status, OAuth-authentication, reload, and configuration-management tools around loaded MCP tools; it serializes revision-based reloads and only retries a reload after cancellation, not after a non-cancellation failure.

Talon's MCP configuration store exposes a redacted HMAC-revision view and performs locked, no-follow, atomic compare-and-swap updates; auto-approved updates that preserve redacted values may not change execution or routing fields other than tool filters.

Talon stores OAuth credentials with endpoint and OAuth-settings isolation, owner-only filesystem modes, locked atomic persistence, absolute expiry, and refresh-token preservation only for refresh responses.
Talon routes OAuth discovery and device authorization through a proxy-ignoring HTTPS-only SSRF-safe client that rejects redirects and validates endpoints before credential-bearing requests.

Talon binds in-channel MCP authorization to an invocation and emits completion/failure status without letting delivery errors undo persisted credentials; runs without a current authorization handler, including scheduled jobs and background subagents, fail with an explicit interactive-login remedy.
